Debt consolidation: compare the monthly relief with the full repayment cost

Use four graphics to compare two existing repayment schedules with a proposed loan, including the effect of a financed setup fee and a longer term.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore debt consolidation and repayment length

Interactive planning lab

Current combined monthly payment$975.68
Proposed monthly payment$431.32
Change in borrowing cost$2,462.65

Hypothetical fixed fully amortizing loans. Both current debts use the selected remaining years; the proposed loan refinances their principal plus its setup fee. Rates are nominal annual rates divided by 12, with month-end payments. Borrowing cost means interest plus the financed setup fee, excluding original debt principal. No new spending, prepayment charges, insurance, promotional periods, rate changes, approval criteria or investment of payment savings is modeled. With zero debt, no new loan or setup fee is assumed.

The central idea

A lower payment can come from a lower rate, a longer repayment period or both. Compare the debt-free date and total interest and fees before interpreting the relief.

01

Start with a complete repayment comparison

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s consolidation guidance describes combining debts and explains that a lower-interest arrangement may still cost more if repayment is extended. It also emphasizes understanding the debts and the terms of a proposed product.

This example begins with two balances and their nominal annual rates. Both current debts are assumed to amortize fully over the selected remaining years. The proposed loan refinances their combined principal and finances its setup fee. These are invented fixed-rate schedules, rather than the minimum-payment rules of actual credit cards or lines of credit.

The default balances are CAD 12,000 at 18% and CAD 8,000 at 12%, each with two years remaining. The proposed alternative is 10% over five years with a CAD 300 financed fee. No rates shown here are offers or estimates of what a lender would approve.

02

Read the payment reduction in its time context

The monthly-payment bars compare the current combined payment with the proposed payment. In the default case, those amounts are CAD 975.68 and CAD 431.32. The difference provides recurring cash-flow relief while the schedules overlap.

However, the current loans finish after 24 payments. The proposed arrangement continues for 60 payments. A comparison that stops at the first month misses those additional three years of obligations. The balance chart therefore keeps both paths visible through the longer horizon.

After a current loan reaches zero, its plotted balance stays at zero. The calculator does not assume the released payment continues into another debt or an investment account. It compares scheduled loan cash flows; it is not a complete comparison of household wealth under different uses of the released money.

03

Compare the cost of borrowing, with principal excluded

Borrowing cost here means interest plus the setup fee, rather than the original principal. The original CAD 20,000 must be repaid in either arrangement, so separating it helps reveal the cost of obtaining and extending the credit.

The default current schedules incur CAD 3,416.25 in interest. The proposed loan incurs CAD 5,878.90 in interest and the financed setup fee combined. Despite its lower rate and monthly payment, the proposed borrowing cost is CAD 2,462.65 higher under these assumptions.

The stacked bars show interest and setup-fee principal separately. Interest charged on that financed fee is already included in the proposed interest amount. Adding the fee to the loan and then counting all loan repayments plus the fee again would count the fee principal twice.

04

Use the matrix to separate the rate and term effects

Each matrix cell recalculates the proposed arrangement at a displayed rate and term while retaining the selected original balances and setup fee. The amount is full-life borrowing cost. Read across a rate row to see the effect of duration, and down a term column to compare rates.

The loan formula uses a monthly rate equal to the nominal annual rate divided by twelve, with payments at month-end. If B is the financed balance, r the monthly rate and n the payment count, the payment is Br ÷ [1 − (1 + r)−n]. At zero interest, it is B ÷ n.

A lender’s actual rate convention, fees, insurance, prepayment terms and variable-rate features can differ. The matrix does not include promotional-rate expiry, additional borrowing or future rate changes. Replacing an existing schedule with a new one requires the actual contractual figures for a meaningful comparison.

05

Connect the proposed schedule with a sustainable budget

A lower monthly obligation can matter when cash flow is tight, even when it increases total cost. Assess that trade-off explicitly: identify the amount of relief, the added repayment years and the change in borrowing cost, then compare them with the household’s available income and flexibility.

The tool assumes no new spending on the cleared accounts. Reusing credit can create a different debt path from the one shown. It also does not assess collateral, credit history, eligibility or the consequences of converting unsecured obligations into secured borrowing.

Review actual balances, payoff amounts, closure costs, proposed terms and an affordable payment schedule. The graphs organize those questions without selecting a provider or determining whether consolidation is appropriate. If the proposed payment still does not fit the budget, changing the loan label does not close that underlying cash-flow gap.

The worked examples, scenario assumptions, and research checklists are TickerLantern’s own educational analysis; they are not source-reported investment results.
